rte-gallipoli-landings.why: The Ottoman Empire had joined the Central Powers in late 1914 and closed the Dardanelles, Russia's main sea route to the Mediterranean. With the Western Front deadlocked, British planners sought another way to strike. A naval attempt to force the straits failed in March 1915, so an army was sent.
rte-gallipoli-landings.impact: Each side suffered roughly a quarter of a million casualties, though estimates vary. The failure damaged Winston Churchill's career for years, while the defence made the reputation of the Ottoman officer Mustafa Kemal, later Atatürk. The campaign became central to national memory in Australia, New Zealand and Turkey.

rte-armistice-compiegne.why: Germany's spring offensives of 1918 had failed and Allied attacks since the summer were pushing its armies back. Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary had already given up. A naval mutiny at Kiel spread into revolution at home, and the Kaiser abdicated two days before the signing.
rte-armistice-compiegne.impact: Germany had to evacuate occupied territory and hand over guns, aircraft, submarines and much of its fleet, while the Allied blockade continued. Peace terms followed in the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. In 1940 Hitler made France sign its own armistice in the same railway carriage.

rte-invasion-of-poland.why: Hitler wanted to overturn the Versailles settlement, which had given Poland a corridor to the sea and made Danzig a free city, and he sought living space in the east. A pact with the Soviet Union in August 1939 secretly divided Poland and removed the risk of Soviet opposition.
rte-invasion-of-poland.impact: Occupation was brutal on both sides of the new line. Around six million Polish citizens died during the war, about half of them Jewish, though estimates vary. A Polish government in exile carried on from abroad, and Polish soldiers, airmen and codebreakers fought alongside the Allies throughout.

rte-operation-dynamo.why: In May 1940 German armour broke through the Ardennes at Sedan and raced to the Channel coast, cutting off the British Expeditionary Force and French armies in the north. A German order halting the tanks for several days, whose reasons are still debated, gave the defenders time to form a perimeter.
rte-operation-dynamo.impact: France fought on for only a few more weeks and signed an armistice on 22 June. Many French troops who held the perimeter were captured. Churchill warned that wars are not won by evacuations, yet the rescue became a lasting British symbol of resilience, the Dunkirk spirit.

rte-pearl-harbor.why: Japan's war in China and its move into French Indochina led the United States to freeze Japanese assets and cut off oil in 1941. Japanese leaders decided to seize the oil and rubber of South-East Asia, and planned to cripple the American fleet first to prevent interference.
rte-pearl-harbor.impact: The American aircraft carriers were at sea and escaped, and the base's fuel stores and repair yards survived, which allowed a quick recovery. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States days later. At home, isolationism collapsed and Japanese Americans were soon forced into internment camps.

rte-ve-day.why: By spring 1945 Allied armies had crossed the Rhine from the west and Soviet forces had fought their way into Berlin. Hitler killed himself on 30 April, leaving Admiral Dönitz to head a brief successor government whose only real task was to arrange surrender.
rte-ve-day.impact: The war against Japan continued until August. Germany was divided into four occupation zones, a split that hardened into two states during the Cold War. Because the surrender took effect after midnight Moscow time, Russia and several neighbours mark Victory Day on 9 May.

rte-sinking-of-lusitania.why: In February 1915 Germany declared the seas around the British Isles a war zone, in response to the British naval blockade, and warned that merchant ships might be sunk on sight. The German embassy even placed warning notices in American newspapers. The liner's cargo included rifle ammunition.
rte-sinking-of-lusitania.impact: More than 120 Americans were among the dead, and after strong protests from Washington Germany limited attacks on passenger ships. The United States stayed neutral for almost two more years. Germany's return to unrestricted submarine warfare in early 1917 was a main reason America finally entered the war.

rte-battle-of-verdun.why: The German commander Erich von Falkenhayn picked a place France would feel bound to defend, a salient ringed by forts that had been stripped of many guns. He later claimed his aim was attrition from the start, though historians debate how far that was planned in advance.
rte-battle-of-verdun.impact: Combined casualties are usually put at around 700,000, with estimates varying. Philippe Pétain emerged as a national hero, and Falkenhayn was replaced by Hindenburg. With French strength tied down, Britain took the larger share of the Somme offensive, and the experience encouraged France's later faith in fixed fortifications.

rte-operation-barbarossa.why: Hitler had long aimed to conquer living space in the east and destroy the Soviet state, and he wanted its grain and oil. The 1939 pact with Stalin was a temporary convenience. Stalin dismissed repeated warnings of attack, so Soviet frontier forces were caught unprepared.
rte-operation-barbarossa.impact: The Soviet Union became an ally of Britain and later the United States, receiving large shipments of supplies. Behind the front, German killing squads murdered Jews in mass shootings, and millions of Soviet prisoners died in captivity. Soviet war deaths are commonly estimated at around 27 million.

rte-second-el-alamein.why: Rommel had driven deep into Egypt in the summer of 1942 but was stopped at the Alamein line, a narrow front between the sea and impassable desert. His supply lines were long and under attack, while Montgomery built up a clear advantage in tanks, guns and aircraft.
rte-second-el-alamein.impact: Days later Anglo-American forces landed in Morocco and Algeria, trapping the Axis between two armies. The last Axis troops in Africa surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943, opening the way to invade Sicily. In Britain church bells, silent since 1940, were rung to mark the victory.

rte-battle-of-tannenberg.why: Germany's war plan sent most of its army west against France, leaving a single army to hold East Prussia. After an early setback its commander was dismissed, and Hindenburg was called out of retirement with Ludendorff as chief of staff. Intercepted uncoded Russian radio messages revealed the enemy's movements.
rte-battle-of-tannenberg.impact: Tens of thousands of Russian soldiers were taken prisoner, and a second victory at the Masurian Lakes cleared East Prussia. Hindenburg and Ludendorff went on to direct Germany's whole war effort from 1916. Hindenburg's fame later carried him to the German presidency in 1925.

rte-battle-of-jutland.why: Britain's navy was blockading Germany from a distance, and the smaller German fleet hoped to lure out and destroy part of it to even the odds. British codebreakers read German signals, so the Grand Fleet under Jellicoe was already at sea before the Germans left harbour.
rte-battle-of-jutland.impact: More than 6,000 British sailors died, yet the blockade held and contributed to severe food shortages in Germany. Unable to win on the surface, Germany turned to unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917. Its idle battle fleet mutinied in 1918, helping to trigger the revolution that ended the war.

rte-battle-of-amiens.why: Germany's spring offensives had cost it many of its best troops without winning the war, and the Allies had regained the initiative in July. The attack was prepared in strict secrecy, with the Canadian Corps moved in at night and no long preliminary bombardment to give warning.
rte-battle-of-amiens.impact: The defeat persuaded Ludendorff that Germany could no longer win. The Allies followed with a rolling series of attacks that broke the Hindenburg Line in late September, and Germany asked for an armistice within weeks. The battle became a model for combining infantry, artillery, tanks and aircraft.

rte-battle-of-kursk.why: After the German defeat at Stalingrad and a recovery around Kharkov, the front was left with a large Soviet-held bulge around Kursk. Hitler wanted to cut it off but delayed for weeks to wait for new heavy tanks. Soviet intelligence gave ample warning of the plan.
rte-battle-of-kursk.impact: Hitler called off the attack after little more than a week, partly because the Allies had landed in Sicily. Soviet counter-offensives then retook Orel, Belgorod and Kharkov in August and reached the Dnieper, liberating Kiev in November. Germany never mounted another major offensive in the east.

rte-battle-of-leyte-gulf.why: American forces under MacArthur landed on Leyte in October 1944 to begin retaking the Philippines. Losing the islands would cut Japan off from the oil of South-East Asia, so its navy committed almost every remaining warship, using carriers with few aircraft as a decoy to draw the Americans away.
rte-battle-of-leyte-gulf.impact: Japan lost the giant battleship Musashi along with its last operational carriers, and its surviving ships were left short of fuel. The Allies went on to retake much of the Philippines in 1945. The night action in Surigao Strait was the last battle fought between battleships.

rte-intel-4004.why: Busicom wanted a set of custom chips for a new calculator. Intel engineer Ted Hoff proposed a single programmable processor instead, and Federico Faggin led the detailed design using new silicon-gate technology. Intel later bought back the rights so it could sell the chip to anyone.
rte-intel-4004.impact: Intel followed it with the 8008 and then the 8080, the chip at the heart of the Altair hobby computer of the mid-1970s. Cheap programmable processors soon spread beyond computers into tills, traffic lights, cars and household appliances, replacing purpose-built circuits with software.

rte-polio-vaccine-safe.why: Polio epidemics had grown worse through the first half of the century, paralysing thousands of children each summer. In 1949 researchers learned to grow the virus in laboratory tissue cultures, making a vaccine practical. Public donations to the March of Dimes funded Salk's work with killed virus.
rte-polio-vaccine-safe.impact: Within weeks a badly made batch from one manufacturer caused cases of polio, which led to much tighter vaccine regulation. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine followed in the early 1960s. A global eradication campaign begun in 1988 has cut cases by more than 99 per cent.

rte-first-mobile-phone-call.why: Car telephones had existed since the 1940s, and Bell Labs had proposed dividing cities into radio cells so frequencies could be reused. AT&T concentrated on phones fitted in vehicles. Motorola wanted to prove a truly portable handset was possible while American regulators were deciding how to allocate frequencies.
rte-first-mobile-phone-call.impact: Commercial cellular networks opened in Japan in 1979 and in the United States in 1983, when Motorola's first handheld went on sale for nearly four thousand dollars. Handsets shrank and prices fell through the 1990s, and mobile subscriptions worldwide now outnumber people.

rte-louise-brown-born.why: Edwards had been studying how to fertilise human eggs outside the body since the 1960s, and Steptoe had pioneered keyhole surgery that could collect eggs from the ovary. Britain's Medical Research Council declined to fund them, so they relied on private money. Many earlier attempts had failed.
rte-louise-brown-born.impact: The birth prompted intense ethical debate. In Britain it led to the Warnock inquiry and, in 1990, a law regulating fertility treatment and embryo research. IVF also made possible later techniques such as egg donation, embryo freezing and genetic testing of embryos before pregnancy.

rte-ibm-pc.why: Small computers from Apple, Commodore and Tandy were selling well by the late 1970s, and spreadsheet software had made them useful in offices. IBM, dominant in large mainframes, risked missing the market. Its team was allowed to bypass normal company procedures and buy in parts such as Intel's processor.
rte-ibm-pc.impact: Compaq and others soon copied the design legally, and IBM lost control of the standard it had created. The lasting winners were Microsoft and Intel, whose software and chips went into almost every compatible machine. IBM sold its personal computer business to Lenovo in 2005.

rte-dolly-the-sheep.why: Frogs had been cloned from tadpole cells in the 1960s, and the Roslin team under Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell had cloned sheep from embryo cells the year before. They hoped to breed livestock that produced medicines in their milk. Dolly was the only lamb from 277 attempts.
rte-dolly-the-sheep.impact: The news set off worldwide debate, and many countries moved to ban human reproductive cloning. Cattle, mice, pigs and other animals were cloned in the following years. The work also encouraged research that showed, in 2006, how adult cells could be turned back into stem cells.

rte-comet-jetliner-service.why: Jet engines had been developed for military aircraft during the Second World War. A wartime British committee planning for peacetime aviation recommended a jet-powered airliner, hoping to challenge American dominance in transport aircraft. De Havilland built the Comet, which first flew in 1949.
rte-comet-jetliner-service.impact: The grounding cost Britain its lead. Boeing's 707 entered service in 1958 and American manufacturers came to dominate the market, although a redesigned Comet flew the first transatlantic jet passenger service that year. Rounded windows and full-scale fatigue testing of fuselages became standard practice.

rte-telstar-launch.why: The idea of relaying signals by satellite dated from the 1940s, and the space race after Sputnik made it achievable. Undersea cables could carry only a limited number of telephone calls and no television. Large ground stations were built in Maine, Cornwall and Brittany to track the satellite.
rte-telstar-launch.impact: Telstar's low orbit meant it could link the continents for only about twenty minutes on each pass, and radiation from high-altitude nuclear tests damaged its electronics within months. Satellites in geostationary orbit, such as Early Bird in 1965, soon provided a permanent link.

rte-arpanet-first-message.why: The United States created its Advanced Research Projects Agency after the shock of Sputnik. Its computing office wanted the researchers it funded to share scarce and expensive machines. The network used packet switching, an idea developed independently by Paul Baran in America and Donald Davies in Britain.
rte-arpanet-first-message.impact: Four sites were connected by the end of 1969. Electronic mail arrived in 1971 and quickly became the most popular use. In 1983 the network switched to the TCP/IP rules that still govern the internet, and ARPANET itself was shut down in 1990.

rte-concorde-service.why: Britain and France were each studying supersonic airliners and agreed by treaty in 1962 to share the enormous cost. National prestige and rivalry with American and Soviet projects drove the programme forward. The prototype first flew in 1969, but development took seven more years.
rte-concorde-service.impact: The first services ran from London to Bahrain and from Paris to Rio de Janeiro. Sonic booms restricted supersonic flight to routes over the sea, and high fuel costs deterred other airlines from buying it. After a fatal crash near Paris in 2000, the fleet retired in 2003.

rte-macintosh-release.why: Researchers at Xerox's Palo Alto laboratory had built computers with windows, icons and a mouse in the 1970s, which Steve Jobs saw on a visit in 1979. Apple's first attempt, the Lisa, was too expensive to sell well. The Macintosh began as a cheaper project that Jobs took over.
rte-macintosh-release.impact: Sales slowed after a strong start, and Jobs left Apple in 1985. That year a laser printer and page layout software made the Macintosh the foundation of desktop publishing. Microsoft's Windows brought a similar way of working to the far larger number of IBM-compatible computers.

rte-insulin-first-patient.why: Experiments in 1889 had shown that removing a dog's pancreas caused diabetes, but earlier attempts to extract the active substance had proved too toxic to use. Banting, a young surgeon, brought a new approach to Macleod's laboratory in Toronto in 1921. Until then the only treatment was a near-starvation diet.
rte-insulin-first-patient.impact: The discoverers sold their patent to the University of Toronto for a token dollar each, and large-scale production began in 1923. A diagnosis that had meant death within months or a few years became a manageable condition. Thompson himself lived another thirteen years.

rte-goddard-rocket.why: Goddard, a physics professor at Clark University, had been experimenting with rockets since the 1910s, supported by small grants from the Smithsonian Institution. He recognised that liquid fuels offered far more energy than gunpowder. A 1919 paper suggesting a rocket could reach the Moon brought him public ridicule.
rte-goddard-rocket.impact: The flight drew little attention at the time. Goddard later moved to Roswell, New Mexico, where he developed gyroscopic steering and fuel pumps for larger rockets. German engineers independently built the liquid-fuelled V-2 during the Second World War, and NASA named a major space centre after Goddard in 1959.

rte-heinkel-he-178.why: Propellers and piston engines were approaching their limits in speed and altitude. Von Ohain patented a jet engine design in 1936 and the aircraft maker Ernst Heinkel funded the work privately. In Britain Frank Whittle had patented his own design in 1930 and was developing it independently.
rte-heinkel-he-178.impact: Britain's first jet, powered by Whittle's engine, flew in 1941. Germany's Messerschmitt Me 262 became the first jet fighter in combat service in 1944, too late to affect the outcome of the war. After 1945 jets rapidly replaced piston engines in fighters, bombers and eventually airliners.

rte-first-implanted-pacemaker.why: Pacemakers of the early 1950s were bulky external machines, some plugged into the mains. The invention of the transistor allowed a circuit small enough to place inside the body. Larsson suffered repeated, life-threatening fainting attacks from a slow heartbeat, and his wife urged the doctors to try.
rte-first-implanted-pacemaker.impact: The first device failed within hours and was replaced by a second. Reliable implantable pacemakers reached patients in the United States from 1960, and lithium batteries introduced in the 1970s extended their life to years. The same technology later led to implantable defibrillators that correct dangerous heart rhythms.
